name: Panama hat

card.summary: The Panama hat is a lightweight woven toquilla-straw hat that adds a classic summer finish to an outfit and shades the face and head.
card.note: Fine hand-woven grades are costly; cheaper imitations exist.

quick.overview:
A Panama hat is a woven straw hat made from the toquilla plant, traditionally in Ecuador despite the name. Its light colour and breathable weave make it a staple of tropical and summer menswear, often paired with linen or silk suits.

For appearance, it frames the face, adds a polished warm-weather accessory and gives shade. Quality is judged by weave fineness, and the finest hats can take months to make.
quick.how: Wearers choose a fedora-style shape and a weave grade, then wear it with summer tailoring or casual beachwear. Finer weaves are lighter and more flexible; cheaper hats use coarser weave or other materials.
quick.risks: No health risks are documented for wearing one. Fine hand-woven hats can cost hundreds to thousands of dollars, and lower-cost machine or foreign-made versions are not equivalent in quality, according to descriptions of the trade.

lead: The Panama hat comes from Ecuador despite its name. It is traditionally made from the plaited leaves of the toquilla or jipijapa plant, Carludovica palmata, and the term appears in print from 1828 [1].

Demand grew during the California Gold Rush, when travellers crossing the Isthmus of Panama needed sun protection, and Theodore Roosevelt's 1906 photograph in one at the Panama Canal boosted its popularity [1]. In the 1920s and 1930s lighter fedora-like Panamas displaced the straw boater as the favoured summer hat [1].

Today the hat is a style accessory: light-coloured and breathable, often worn with linen or silk summer suits [1]. UNESCO added the traditional weaving art to its Intangible Cultural Heritage list in December 2012 [1].

angle.text: The hat completes a warm-weather outfit and shades the face. Wearers pick brim and shape to suit their face and style.

infobox: About $450 to $10,000 abroad for fine hats
Measured in weave tightness; Montecristi is the finest

paras: Quality depends on how tight the weave is, measured with a frame tool and counted in carreras. The best hats, called Montecristis, can have up to 3,000 weaves per square inch [1]. A master weaver may spend up to eight months on one hat [1].

Spanish conquistadors saw coastal Ecuadorians in toquilla-straw hats in 1526, and hat weaving was a cottage industry by the mid-1600s [1]. About 220,000 hats a year were imported to the US by 1850, and they were shown at the 1855 Paris World's Fair [1].
